questions.question: Room 8 at Maple Grove Elementary made a pictograph of the recess activity each student picked. The key says: each circle stands for 1 student. Soccer: 9 circles. Basketball: 6 circles. Tag: 7 circles. Skipping: 4 circles. Which activity was picked by exactly 7 students?
questions.explain: When one symbol stands for 1, the number of symbols in a row IS the number of students, so find the row with 7 circles: Tag. The common trap is grabbing the tallest or the first row instead of counting the row that matches the number asked for.

questions.question: Nina collected this data table about how her class travels to school. Walk: 6 students. Bus: 9 students. Car: 4 students. Bike: 3 students. She is drawing a bar graph where each square stands for 1 student. How tall should the bar for ‘Bus’ be?
questions.explain: With a one-to-one graph, you draw one square for each student, so 9 students means a bar 9 squares tall. The common trap is drawing the total of all four rows (22) or copying the number from the wrong row.

questions.question: On a pictograph of salmon spotted in the Capilano River, the key says: each fish symbol stands for 5 salmon. Tuesday’s row has 4 fish symbols. What does Tuesday’s row tell you?
questions.explain: Each symbol counts as 5, so 4 symbols means 4 groups of 5, which is 4 × 5 = 20 salmon. The most common mistake is counting the symbols as 4 (ignoring the key) or adding 4 + 5 instead of multiplying.

questions.question: Jayden is making a pictograph of juice boxes sold at the school fair. His key says: each cup symbol stands for 5 juice boxes. On Saturday, 35 juice boxes were sold. How many cup symbols should Jayden draw in Saturday’s row?
questions.explain: To go from real amounts back to symbols you divide by the key: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 symbols. The common trap is drawing 35 symbols (forgetting the key works both ways) or adding and subtracting 5 instead of dividing.

questions.question: A Grade 4 class in Kelowna graphed the bottles they collected for recycling. Each square on the bar graph stands for 5 bottles. Week 1: 6 squares. Week 2: 4 squares. Week 3: 9 squares. Week 4: 7 squares. How many more bottles did they collect in Week 3 than in Week 2?
questions.explain: Find the difference in squares first (9 − 4 = 5 squares), then use the key: 5 × 5 = 25 bottles. The biggest trap is answering 5 by forgetting the key, or adding the two bars (9 + 4) when the question says ‘how many more’.

questions.question: The lost-and-found bin at school was emptied and the items were shown on a bar graph where each square stands for 1 item. Mitts: 8. Toques: 5. Water bottles: 11. Jackets: 6. How many items were in the bin altogether?
questions.explain: Read every bar and add them all: 8 + 5 + 11 + 6 = 30 items. Common traps are losing a ten while regrouping (29) or forgetting to include one of the four bars.

questions.question: Riverside School ran a muffin sale. The bar graph shows muffins sold, and each square stands for 5 muffins. Monday: 4 squares. Tuesday: 6 squares. Wednesday: 3 squares. Thursday: 7 squares. Every muffin was sold for $2. How much money did the sale make on Tuesday and Thursday together?
questions.explain: Two steps: change squares to muffins with the key (6 × 5 = 30 and 7 × 5 = 35, so 65 muffins), then multiply by the price: 65 × $2 = $130. The usual traps are using the squares as muffins ($26) or stopping after finding 65 muffins and forgetting the $2 price.

questions.question: Two classes made pictographs of the laps they ran on Track Day. Division 5’s key says each shoe stands for 2 laps, and their row has 8 shoes. Division 6’s key says each shoe stands for 5 laps, and their row has 5 shoes. Ali says, ‘Division 5 ran more, because their row has more shoes.’ Who really ran more laps, and by how many?
options: They ran the same number of laps
questions.explain: You cannot compare rows until you use each key: Division 5 ran 8 × 2 = 16 laps and Division 6 ran 5 × 5 = 25 laps, so Division 6 ran 25 − 16 = 9 more. Ali fell into the most common trap in this unit — comparing the number of symbols when the two graphs have different keys.
